title: Crop Selection and Rotation
summary: Learn how to pick crops that match your land and climate, and how to rotate them to keep soil healthy. This lesson shows simple steps for planning effective crop rotations.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Crops
sections.body:
First look at your climate, soil type, and water availability. Some crops, like wheat, need cool, dry conditions, while others, like rice, thrive in warm, wet fields.

Next consider market demand and your farming goals. Growing vegetables for a local market may be more profitable than a grain that is sold far away.

Finally, check the crop's nutrient needs. Crops that use a lot of nitrogen, such as corn, should be balanced with legumes that add nitrogen back to the soil.

sections.heading: Why Rotate Crops?
sections.body:
Crop rotation breaks pest and disease cycles. When the same plant is grown year after year, pests that like that plant can build up and cause big losses.

Rotating also improves soil structure and fertility. Different roots reach different soil layers, and some plants leave behind organic matter that feeds soil microbes.

A simple rotation might be: legumes → leafy greens → root vegetables → grain. This pattern moves nitrogen‑fixing plants, leafy crops, and deep‑rooted crops through the field.

sections.heading: Planning a Simple Rotation
sections.body:
Start by drawing a field map and dividing it into three or four sections. Assign each section a crop from your rotation plan.

Every year move each crop to the next section. Over a four‑year cycle, every part of the field will have grown each type of crop once.

Keep records of yields, pest problems, and soil tests. Over time you can adjust the order or add new crops to improve results.

quiz.q: Which factor is NOT essential when choosing a crop?
quiz.why: Crop choice depends on climate, soil, and market, not personal color preferences.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of planting legumes in a rotation?
options: They produce a lot of fruit
They fix nitrogen in the soil
quiz.why: Legumes host bacteria that convert atmospheric nitrogen into usable forms.

quiz.q: A four‑year rotation includes legumes, leafy greens, root vegetables, and grain. Which crop should follow legumes?
quiz.why: Leafy greens benefit from the nitrogen left by the preceding legume.

quiz.q: Why does rotating crops help control pests?
options: It removes the host plant for a season
quiz.why: Pests that specialize on one crop lose their food source when that crop is rotated out.
